title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt III: Beowulf Sets Sail (lines 189–257)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 8–10, lines 189–257 (fitt III). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Swā ðā mǣlceare maga Healfdenes
singāla sēað;
sentences.l: So then with the time-care the kinsman of Healfdene continually seethed;
sentences.i: So the son of Healfdene seethed without ceasing, with the grief that came upon him again and again;
sentences.n: The subject ‘maga Healfdenes’ (‘kinsman of Healfdene’, here the son) is Hrothgar, the second of the four children Fitt I names; the poem lets his name wait. ‘mǣlceare’ is a dative of means: he seethes ‘by means of’ the care. ‘mǣlcearu’ is a compound found only here; ‘mǣl’ is ‘time, appointed moment’, so ‘time-care’ is a guess at ‘sorrow that returns at its times’. ‘sēað’ is the past tense of ‘sēoþan’, ‘to boil’, the verb for a pot, and our ‘seethe’. The poem pictures grief as heat working inside a man.

sentences.t:
ne mihte snotọr hæleð
wēan onwendan;
sentences.l: not could the wise hero woe turn-away;
sentences.i: and the wise man could not turn the woe aside;
sentences.n: ‘ne mihte … onwendan’ is ‘could not turn away’: the verb ‘mihte’ takes a bare infinitive, and the object ‘wēan’ comes between them. The dot under the vowel in ‘snotọr’ is Klaeber's sign that this vowel does not count in the metre; the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there. ‘snotor’ means ‘wise, prudent’, the old praise-word for a counsellor-king. ‘wēan’ is the accusative of ‘wēa’, ‘woe’.

sentences.t:
wæs þæt gewin tō swȳð,
lāþ ond longsum, þē on ðā lēode becōm,
nȳdwracu nīþgrim, nihtbealwa mǣst.
sentences.l: that struggle was too strong, loathsome and long-lasting, that came on the people, a compulsion-affliction, malice-grim, of night-bales the greatest.
sentences.i: That struggle was too great: hateful and long-lasting, the cruel oppression, savage in its malice, that came upon the people, the worst of night-evils.
sentences.n: ‘þē’ after the comma is a relative particle, ‘that, which’, and its verb is ‘becōm’ (‘came’): the struggle ‘that came on the people’. ‘lāþ ond longsum’ repeats the formula Fitt II used of the same years. ‘nȳdwracu’ is ‘compulsion-affliction’ (‘nȳd’ is need, force), and ‘nīþgrim’ is ‘malice-grim’ (‘nīþ’ is hostility). ‘nihtbealwa mǣst’ is ‘of night-bales the greatest’: a genitive plural of ‘bealu’, ‘evil’, the word in ‘morðbealu’ in Fitt II. Fitt II puts Grendel's first raid ‘syþðan niht becōm’, ‘after night came’.

sentences.t:
Þæt fram hām gefrægn Higelāces þegn
gōd mid Gēatum, Grendles dǣda;
sentences.l: That from home heard Higelac's thane, good among the Geats, Grendel's deeds;
sentences.i: Far from there, at home, Higelac's thane, a good man among the Geats, heard of Grendel's deeds;
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the object of ‘gefrægn’ (‘heard’), and ‘Grendles dǣda’ stands beside it as an explanation: ‘that, Grendel's deeds’. ‘gefrægn’ is the past tense of ‘gefrignan’, ‘to learn by asking, to hear told’, the poet's usual word for what he has from report; ‘fram hām’ is literally ‘from home’; it is read here as ‘away from the scene, at home’, which is a choice. The poet calls the hero only ‘Higelāces þegn’, ‘thane of Higelac’ (Higelāc is the Geat king). The Geats are a people of what is now southern Sweden.

sentences.t:
sē wæs moncynnes mægenes strengest
on þǣm dæge þysses līfes,
æþele ond ēacen.
sentences.l: he was of mankind in might the strongest on that day of this life, noble and mighty.
sentences.i: He was the strongest of mankind in might, in that day, in this life, noble and mighty.
sentences.n: Two genitives lean on the superlative: ‘moncynnes’ (‘of mankind’) and ‘mægenes’ (‘in might’). ‘on þǣm dæge þysses līfes’ is ‘on that day of this life’, the poet's way of saying ‘in his own time, in this world’. ‘ēacen’ is the past participle of ‘ēacan’, ‘to increase’, so ‘swelled, mighty’; it describes size as well as power. The praise is given while the man is still unnamed.

sentences.t:
Hēt him ȳðlidan
gōdne gegyrwan;
sentences.l: Commanded for himself a wave-goer, a good one, to make ready;
sentences.i: He ordered a good ship to be made ready for him;
sentences.n: ‘Hēt’ (‘commanded’) takes an accusative and an infinitive: ‘commanded a ship to be got ready’, with no one named as the doer. ‘him’ is a dative of interest, ‘for himself’. ‘ȳðlida’ is ‘wave-goer’, a kenning for ship; it is a noun formed from ‘līðan’, ‘to travel by water’, which comes back in ‘līðende’ (221) and ‘liden’ (223). A kenning is a compound that names a thing by what it does, and later notes only nudge when one returns.

sentences.t:
cwæð, hē gūðcyning
ofer swanrāde sēcean wolde,
mǣrne þēoden, þā him wæs manna þearf.
sentences.l: said, he the war-king over the swan-road seek would, the famed lord, since to him was of men need.
sentences.i: and said that he would seek out the warrior-king over the swan's road, that famed lord, since the king had need of men.
sentences.n: After ‘cwæð’ the reported statement has its own subject: ‘he would seek the war-king’. The king is the object, and his two names ‘gūðcyning’ and ‘mǣrne þēoden’ are accusative singular, a pair of titles for one man. In ‘þā him wæs manna þearf’ (‘since to him was need of men’; ‘þā’ can also be ‘when’) the ‘him’ is the king, the one in need, and ‘manna’ is a genitive of the thing needed. ‘swanrād’ is the swan's road, a sea-kenning like the prologue's ‘hronrād’ (‘whale-road’); the swan is the bird at home on water.

sentences.t:
Ðone sīðfæt him snotere ceorlas
lȳthwōn lōgon, þēah hē him lēof wǣre;
sentences.l: That journey for him wise men little blamed, though he to them dear were;
sentences.i: The wise men found little fault with that venture of his, though he was dear to them;
sentences.n: ‘lȳthwōn’ is ‘a little’, and ‘lōgon’ (past of ‘lēan’, ‘to blame’) takes the thing blamed in the accusative, ‘Ðone sīðfæt’, and the person in the dative, ‘him’. The words are understatement: ‘blamed him little’ means ‘did not blame him’. ‘wǣre’ is subjunctive, ‘though he were dear’, and this ‘him’ is the wise men: they love him and still let him go. ‘ceorlas’ here is ‘freemen’; the word is the ancestor of ‘churl’. ‘snotere’ is the plural of ‘snotor’, ‘wise’, used of Hrothgar at 190.

sentences.t: hwetton hige(r)ōfne, hǣl scēawedon.
sentences.l: They whetted the mind-bold one, looked at omens.
sentences.i: They spurred on the bold-hearted man and studied the omens.
sentences.n: ‘hwetton’ is ‘whetted’, as one sharpens a blade; here it means ‘urged on’. The subject, still the wise men, is not repeated. ‘hige(r)ōfne’ is ‘mind-bold’, the accusative of ‘higerōf’, with ‘hige’ ‘mind’ and ‘rōf’ ‘bold’. The parentheses are Klaeber's: the manuscript is damaged here, and the letter ‘r’ is restored. The two 1787 Thorkelin transcripts read ‘þofne’ (A) and ‘forne’ (B), and the restoration ‘-rōfne’ is Rask's. ‘hǣl’ is a sign or omen of good fortune; the Geats take omens before the voyage.

sentences.l: Had the good one of the Geat-people champions chosen of those that he boldest find could;
sentences.i: The good man of the Geat people had picked out champions, the boldest he could find;
sentences.n: ‘Hæfde … gecorone’ is the old perfect, ‘had chosen’, with the participle agreeing with ‘cempan’ (‘champions’). ‘þāra þe’ is ‘of those whom’, and ‘cēnoste’ is the superlative of ‘cēne’, ‘bold, keen’. ‘Gēata lēoda’ is read here as ‘of the Geat people’, with ‘lēoda’ a genitive plural. This is a guess from the grammar: ‘lēod’ can also mean ‘prince’, which would give ‘the good one, prince of the Geats’. The poet again leaves the hero unnamed and calls him ‘se gōda’, ‘the good one’.

sentences.t:
fīftȳna sum
sundwudu sōhte, secg wīsade,
lagucræftig mon landgemyrcu.
sentences.l: one of fifteen sought the sound-wood, a man showed the way, the sea-skilled man, the land-marks.
sentences.i: One of fifteen, he made for the ship, and a seaman skilled in the water's ways pointed out the landmarks.
sentences.n: ‘fīftȳna sum’ is ‘one of fifteen’: ‘sum’ means ‘one’ and takes a genitive plural, so the leader counts himself, and fourteen men sail with him. The manuscript writes the number as ‘.xv.’ with ‘na’ written above; Klaeber spells it out. ‘sundwudu’ is ‘sound-wood’: ‘sund’ is swimming or a stretch of water, and ‘wudu’, ‘wood’, stands for the timber ship. The man who ‘wīsade’ (‘showed the way’) is ‘lagucræftig’, ‘skilled in the water’ (‘lagu’ is water or sea); The poem leaves the guide unnamed; ‘the ship's pilot’ is a guess. ‘landgemyrcu’ are the land-boundaries; ‘coast marks a seaman steers by’ is the sense taken here, a guess.

sentences.t:
Fyrst forð gewāt; flota wæs on ȳðum,
bāt under beorge.
sentences.l: Time forth went; the floater was on the waves, the boat under the cliff.
sentences.i: Time passed on; the ship rode the waves, the boat under the cliff.
sentences.n: ‘Fyrst’ is a span of time, as in Fitt II's ‘næs hit lengra fyrst’. ‘flota’ is ‘floater’, another ship-word after ‘ȳðlida’ and ‘sundwudu’. ‘ȳðum’ is a dative plural, ‘on the waves’. ‘bāt under beorge’ restates the ship in other words, a way the poem likes to say a thing twice. ‘beorg’ is a hill or mound; ‘cliff’ is a guess for the rise above the landing.

sentences.l: Men ready onto the prow stepped, — currents wound, sea against sand;
sentences.i: The ready warriors climbed aboard at the prow, while the currents swirled, the sea against the sand;
sentences.n: ‘Beornas gearwe’ is ‘men ready’, the adjective set after its noun. ‘stefn’ is the stem or prow. The dash is Klaeber's: it sets the next clause beside the boarding, so the swirling water belongs to the same moment. ‘strēamas wundon’ is ‘currents wound’ (from ‘windan’, ‘to twist’), and ‘sund wið sande’ gives the sea ‘against’ the sand. ‘strēamas’, ‘sund’ and ‘sande’ all begin with ‘s’, and ‘wið’ sits between the last two.

sentences.l: men bore into the bosom of the boat bright trappings, war-gear splendid;
sentences.i: The men carried bright trappings into the ship's hold, splendid war-gear;
sentences.n: ‘on bearm nacan’ is ‘into the bosom of the boat’ (‘nacan’ is the genitive of ‘naca’), the same picture as the prologue's ship-funeral; ‘bearm’ is a lap or bosom. ‘frætwe’ are ornaments and fittings, and ‘gūðsearo geatolīc’ (‘war-gear splendid’) explains them: war-gear counts as treasure as well as equipment.

sentences.t:
guman ūt scufon,
weras on wilsīð wudu bundenne.
sentences.l: men shoved out, warriors on a desired journey, the bound wood.
sentences.i: The men shoved out the well-bound vessel and set off on the voyage they had longed for.
sentences.n: ‘ūt scufon’ is ‘shoved out’, with the object ‘wudu bundenne’ (‘bound wood’) at the end: a ship whose planks are fastened together. ‘wilsīð’ is ‘desired-journey’, with ‘wil-’ from ‘willa’, ‘wish’; ‘a journey they wanted’ is a guess for this compound. ‘guman’ and ‘weras’ are two more words for ‘men’, a pair that the poet uses to vary one subject.

sentences.t:
Gewāt þā ofer wǣgholm winde gefȳsed
flota fāmīheals fugle gelīcost,
sentences.l: Went then over the wave-sea, by wind urged-on, the floater foamy-necked, to a bird most like,
sentences.i: Then the ship went out over the wave-sea, driven on by the wind, foam at its neck, most like a bird,
sentences.n: The subject, ‘flota’, is held back to the second line, so the verb ‘gewāt’ comes first. ‘gefȳsed’ is the participle of ‘fȳsan’, ‘to hasten, drive’, and ‘winde’ is the dative of means. ‘wǣgholm’ is ‘wave-sea’ (‘holm’ is the open sea). ‘fāmīheals’ is ‘foamy-necked’, and the neck is taken to be the curve of the bow throwing spray, a guess. ‘fugle gelīcost’ is ‘most like to a bird’: ‘gelīc’ takes the dative, and the ship flies over the water.

sentences.t:
oð þæt ymb āntīd ōþres dōgọres
wundenstefna gewaden hæfde,
þæt ðā līðende land gesāwon,
brimclifu blīcan, beorgas stēape,
sīde sǣnæssas;
sentences.l: until that about one-time of the second day the wound-prowed one had waded, that the seafarers land saw, sea-cliffs gleaming, hills steep, broad sea-headlands;
sentences.i: until, at about the same hour on the second day, the curved-prowed ship had made so much way that the voyagers saw land: sea-cliffs gleaming, steep hills, broad headlands;
sentences.n: ‘oð þæt … gewaden hæfde’ is ‘until it had waded’, and ‘þæt … gesāwon’ is the result: ‘so that they saw’. The dot under the vowel in ‘dōgọres’ is the same metrical sign as in ‘snotọr’. ‘ymb āntīd’ is uncertain; ‘ān’ is ‘one’ and ‘tīd’ is ‘time’, so ‘at the same hour’ of the second day is the reading taken here, and it is a guess. ‘wundenstefna’ is ‘wound-prow’, a ship whose stem curves; ‘wadan’ is ‘to go through water’. ‘līðende’ are ‘travelers by water’. ‘brimclifu blīcan’ is ‘sea-cliffs gleaming’, the infinitive after ‘gesāwon’ (‘saw … shine’). ‘sīde’ is ‘broad’, and ‘sǣnæssas’ are ‘sea-nesses’, headlands running out into the sea.

sentences.t:
þā wæs sund liden,
eoletes æt ende.
sentences.l: then was the sea crossed, at the end of the eolet.
sentences.i: Then the sea-passage was done, at the end of the voyage.
sentences.n: ‘þā wæs sund liden’ is a passive with ‘sund’ as its subject: ‘then the sea-passage was traveled’, with ‘liden’ the participle of ‘līðan’. ‘eoletes’ is a word found nowhere else, and Klaeber's apparatus lists a string of editors' attempts: ‘ēalāde’, ‘ēalondes’, ‘eodores’, ‘eosetes’, ‘ēares’, ‘ēoledes’. The ‘voyage’ sense is a guess from the context, which is why ‘eolet’ is left untranslated in the literal line.

sentences.t:
Þanon ūp hraðe
Wedera lēode on wang stigon,
sǣwudu sǣldon, — syrcan hrysedon,
gūðgewǣdo;
sentences.l: Thence up quickly the Weders' people onto the plain stepped, the sea-wood moored, — mail-shirts shook, war-garments;
sentences.i: From there the Weders went quickly up onto the land and moored their sea-wood; their mail-shirts rattled, their war-gear;
sentences.n: ‘Wedera lēode’ is ‘people of the Weders’, a second name for the Geats; the poem uses both. ‘wang’ is an open stretch of ground. ‘sǣldon’ is from ‘sǣlan’, ‘to fasten with a rope’ (‘sǣl’ is a rope), so they tie the ship up. ‘sǣwudu’ is ‘sea-wood’, the same kind of ship-name as ‘sundwudu’ at 208. The dash is Klaeber's and marks a short stop before the ring of the armor: ‘syrcan’, mail-shirts, are the subject of ‘hrysedon’ (‘shook’), and ‘gūðgewǣdo’ (‘war-garments’) is a second word for the same things.

sentences.t:
Gode þancedon
þæs þe him ȳþlāde ēaðe wurdon.
sentences.l: God they thanked, for that to them wave-paths easy became.
sentences.i: They thanked God that the wave-ways had proved easy for them.
sentences.n: ‘Gode’ is a dative, since ‘þancian’ takes the dative of the one thanked. ‘þæs þe’ means ‘for that, because’; the genitive gives the reason for the thanks. ‘ȳþlād’ is ‘wave-way’, a sea-kenning in the pattern of ‘swanrād’. ‘ēaðe’ means ‘easy’, and ‘wurdon’ is ‘became’. The poem's narrator is a Christian looking back on pagan-age sailors, and he lets them thank the one God.

sentences.t:
Þā of wealle geseah weard Scildinga,
sē þe holmclifu healdan scolde,
beran ofer bolcan beorhte randas,
fyrdsearu fūslicu;
sentences.l: Then from the wall saw the guardian of the Scyldings, he who the sea-cliffs to hold was to, carry over the gangway bright shields, army-gear ready;
sentences.i: Then the Scyldings' watchman, whose duty was to guard the sea-cliffs, saw from the wall bright shields carried over the gangway, and war-gear all ready;
sentences.n: The main verb is ‘geseah’, and what he sees is a phrase of object plus infinitive: ‘beran … randas’, ‘shields carried’. The relative clause ‘sē þe … healdan scolde’ says ‘who was to hold, whose job was to hold’ the cliffs. ‘Scildinga’ is the Scyldings, Hrothgar's Danes, spelled here with ‘i’. ‘weall’ is ‘wall’ and may mean a cliff-face or an earthwork on the cliff; ‘bolca’ is a plank or gangway, and ‘gangway’ is a guess. ‘rand’ is the rim of a shield, so ‘randas’ are shields. ‘fyrdsearu fūslicu’ is ‘army-gear ready’; Sievers (with a query) and Holthausen read ‘fūslīc’, with a long ī.

sentences.t:
hine fyrwyt bræc
mōdgehygdum, hwæt þā men wǣron.
sentences.l: him curiosity broke in mind-thoughts, what those men were.
sentences.i: Curiosity racked his mind, wondering who those men were.
sentences.n: ‘hine’ is the accusative: curiosity ‘broke’ (‘bræc’, past of ‘brecan’) him, as a pain wears at a man. ‘fyrwyt’ is ‘curiosity’ (‘wit’ is knowledge; ‘fyr-’ is perhaps ‘far, forward’, a guess). ‘mōdgehygdum’ is a dative plural, ‘in his mind-thoughts’. The question ‘hwæt þā men wǣron’ is indirect, with ‘hwæt’ as ‘what (sort of)’; ‘wǣron’ is a plural past, indicative or subjunctive in form, and here may be read ‘might be’. The same ‘hwæt’ opens his own speech.

sentences.t:
Gewāt him þā tō waroðe wicge rīdan
þegn Hrōðgāres, þrymmum cwehte
mægenwudu mundum, meþelwordum frægn:
sentences.l: Went him then to the shore on a steed to ride Hrothgar's thane, with force he shook the might-wood in hands, with meeting-words asked:
sentences.i: Then Hrothgar's thane rode on his horse to the shore, shook his mighty spear in his hands, and asked in formal words:
sentences.n: ‘Gewāt him … rīdan’ is ‘went himself, to ride’: ‘him’ is a reflexive dative and ‘wicge rīdan’ is an infinitive after a verb of motion, ‘went riding’, with ‘wicg’ in the dative, ‘on a steed’. The watchman is the ‘weard Scildinga’ of 229 and the ‘þegn Hrōðgāres’ here, one man with two names. ‘mægenwudu’ is ‘might-wood’, a kenning for the spear, and ‘þrymmum’ is ‘with force’ (‘þrymm’ is strength). ‘meþelwordum’ is ‘with meeting-words’, formal speech of the kind spoken at an assembly; the poet's later ‘maþelode’ has the same root. ‘frægn’ is the plain form of the verb in ‘gefrægn’ (194): ‘asked’. A colon ends the unit, and the next unit starts the speech.

sentences.t:
‘Hwæt syndon gē searohæbbendra,
byrnum werede, þē þus brontne cēol
ofer lagustrǣte lǣdan cwōmon,
hider ofer holmas?
sentences.l: ‘What are you of armor-holders, with byrnies clad, who thus a high keel over the sea-street to lead came, hither over the seas?
sentences.i: ‘Who are you, armed men in your mail, who have come thus, steering a towering ship over the sea-lane, hither across the waters?
sentences.n: The opening quotation mark starts the coastguard's speech, which runs to 257. ‘Hwæt’ here is the question word ‘what’ (the poem's first line has it as the call for attention): ‘hwæt syndon gē searohæbbendra’ is ‘what (kind) are you of armor-holders’, with a partitive genitive. ‘searohæbbendra’ is ‘armor-holders’. ‘byrnum werede’ is ‘clad in byrnies’, and ‘byrne’ is a shirt of mail. ‘þē’ is the relative ‘who’. ‘brontne cēol’ is ‘high keel’; ‘cēol’ is a ship, and ‘lagustrǣte’ is ‘sea-street’, with ‘strǣt’ borrowed from Latin ‘strata’, a paved road.

sentences.t:
[Hwæt, ic hwī]le wæs
endesǣta, ǣgwearde hēold,
þē on land Dena lāðra nǣnig
mid scipherge sceðþan ne meahte.
sentences.l: [What! I for a] while was an end-sitter, watch I held, so that on the land of the Danes of the hateful ones none with a ship-host to harm could not.
sentences.i: Listen! For some time I have been the coast's watchman and held the sea-watch, so that no enemy with a fleet might do harm to the land of the Danes.
sentences.n: The square brackets are Klaeber's: the manuscript is lost here, and the words ‘Hwæt, ic hwī’ are an editor's guess (Sievers). Klaeber's apparatus lists others: [hwīle ic on weal]le (Bu.), [ic hwī]le (Kal., Schü.), [ic on hyl]le (Tr.). ‘hwīle’, ‘for a while’, is common to the first three; ‘Hwæt’ here would be the call for attention, ‘Listen!’. ‘endesǣta’ is ‘end-sitter’, one who sits at the land's edge. ‘ǣgwearde’ is ‘ǣg-ward’; the first part is uncertain, and ‘sea-watch’ is a guess. ‘þē’ opens a clause of result or purpose, ‘so that’, as the manuscript has it, though Thorkelin and others emended it to ‘þæt’. ‘nǣnig … ne meahte’ piles two negatives that reinforce one another, as Old English does: ‘none could not’ means ‘none could’. ‘lāðra’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the hateful ones’, depending on ‘nǣnig’. ‘sceðþan’ is ‘to harm’ (our ‘scathe’).

sentences.t:
Nō hēr cūðlīcor cuman ongunnon
lindhæbbende, nē gē lēafnesword
gūðfremmendra gearwe ne wisson,
māga gemēdu.
sentences.l: Not here more openly to come began shield-holders, nor you leave-word of war-doers clearly not knew, kinsmen's gemēdu.
sentences.i: Never have shield-bearing men come here more openly, nor did you know for certain the warriors' word of leave, the kinsmen's consent.
sentences.n: ‘Nō’ is ‘not at all’, and with the past tense ‘Nō … cuman ongunnon’ reads ‘never began to come’, where ‘ongunnon’ is a helping verb; ‘gearwe’ is the adverb ‘clearly’; ‘cūðlīcor’ is the comparative of ‘cūðlīce’, ‘openly, knowingly’ (‘cūð’ is ‘known’). ‘lindhæbbende’ are ‘shield-holders’ (‘lind’ is lime-wood, hence shield). ‘nē … ne wisson’ is ‘nor … did not know’, two negatives that make one. ‘lēafnesword’ is the ‘word of leave’, permission, and ‘gūðfremmendra’ is ‘of war-doers’, fighting men. ‘māga gemēdu’ is a hard phrase. ‘gemēdu’ may be from ‘gemēde’, ‘pleasing, agreeable’, and so ‘assent’, and ‘consent’ is a guess. It is in apposition to ‘lēafnesword’, saying the same thing in other words.

sentences.l: Never I greater saw of earls on earth, than is of-you one, a man in war-gear;
sentences.i: Never have I seen a greater man among the warriors on earth than one of you, a man in his armor;
sentences.n: ‘māran’ is ‘greater’, the accusative of ‘māra’; ‘eorla’ is a genitive plural, ‘of earls’; and ‘ofer eorþan’ is ‘over the earth’, meaning anywhere. ‘ðonne is ēower sum’ is ‘than is one of you’: ‘sum’ takes a genitive again, as in ‘fīftȳna sum’. ‘secg on searwum’ is ‘a man in war-gear’, and ‘searu’ is armor, cunning-work. The coastguard singles out ‘ēower sum’, one of the company.

sentences.t:
nis þæt seldguma,
wǣpnum geweorðad, næfne him his wlite lēoge,
ǣnlīc ansȳn.
sentences.l: that is not a hall-man, with weapons honored, unless to him his looks lie, an unmatched face.
sentences.i: That is no hall-man graced with weapons, unless his looks speak falsely of him, that matchless appearance.
sentences.n: ‘nis’ is ‘ne is’, ‘is not’. ‘seldguma’ is uncertain: older editors printed two words, ‘seld guma’, ‘rare man’ (cf. ‘seldom’), and Grein joined it into one; ‘hall-man’, a retainer who stays at home, is the reading taken here, a guess. ‘wǣpnum geweorðad’ is ‘honored with weapons’. The letters ‘ne’ in ‘næfne’ are printed in italic, which is Klaeber's mark that he has changed the manuscript: the manuscript has ‘næfre’ (‘never’), and Kemble's ‘næfne’ gives ‘unless’. ‘him his wlite lēoge’ is a subjunctive, ‘unless his looks should lie to him’; the dative ‘him’ is read in the idiomatic line as ‘about him’, a guess. ‘ǣnlīc ansȳn’ (‘unmatched appearance’) names the looks, in the poem's habit of saying a thing twice.

sentences.t:
Nū ic ēower sceal
frumcyn witan, ǣr gē fyr heonan
lēasscēaweras on land Dena
furþur fēran.
sentences.l: Now I of-you must origin know, before you farther from here, false-lookers, into the land of the Danes farther go.
sentences.i: Now I must know your origin, before you go any farther from here into the Danes' land as spies.
sentences.n: ‘Nū ic ēower sceal frumcyn witan’ is ‘now I must know your first-kin’: ‘sceal’ with the infinitive ‘witan’ (‘know’) gives ‘must’, and ‘ēower’ is the genitive of ‘gē’, used as ‘your’. ‘frumcyn’ is the ‘first kin’, one's family and origin. ‘ǣr gē … fēran’ is ‘before you travel’, with ‘fyr’ and ‘furþur’ both meaning ‘farther’. ‘lēasscēaweras’ is ‘false-lookers’, men who pretend to come in peace to look over the ground. Several editors print ‘lēase’ for ‘lēass-’.

sentences.t:
Nū gē feorbūend,
merelīðende, mīn[n]e gehȳrað
ānfealdne geþōht:
sentences.l: Now you far-dwellers, sea-farers, my single thought hear:
sentences.i: Now, you who dwell far off, you sea-farers, hear my plain thought:
sentences.n: ‘gehȳrað’ is the plural imperative, ‘hear!’. ‘feorbūend’ is ‘far-dwellers’ and ‘merelīðende’ is ‘sea-travelers’ (‘mere’ is sea), two plural vocatives. The square brackets in ‘mīn[n]e’ are Klaeber's: the manuscript has ‘mine’, and Kemble added the second ‘n’ so that the adjective agrees with the masculine ‘geþōht’. ‘ānfealdne’ is ‘one-fold’, so ‘single, plain’. The colon says that the thought follows.

sentences.t:
ofost is sēlest
tō gecȳðanne, hwanan ēowre cyme syndon.’
sentences.l: haste is best to declare, whence your comings are.’
sentences.i: Haste is best for declaring whence you have come.’
sentences.n: ‘tō gecȳðanne’ is the inflected infinitive, ‘for making known’: ‘ofost is sēlest’ (‘haste is best’) leads into it. ‘hwanan’ is ‘from where’, and ‘ēowre cyme syndon’ is a plural, ‘your arrivals are’. The closing quotation mark ends the coastguard's speech.
